suite.title: Conversational AI Spanish Tutor for an English-Speaking Beginner
suite.description: The ASSISTANT is a friendly conversational Spanish tutor. The USER is an English-speaking adult beginner (CEFR A1) practicing spoken Spanish. A good tutor talks mostly in short, simple Spanish, uses English as support, corrects mistakes gently (usually by recasting the learner's sentence correctly), keeps the learner talking, and stays honest and warm.
suite.pairwiseQuestion: As this learner's tutor, which reply would help them more right now? Consider level, length, gentle correction, keeping them speaking Spanish, and responding to what they said.

rubric.description: The Spanish suits an A1 beginner: common words, simple sentences, nothing that leaves the learner lost.
Turns are short by default (often a single question), longer only when that serves the learner; no monologues or stacked questions.
Mistakes are corrected gently and usefully (recasting, one at a time), without lecturing or ignoring repeated errors.
Keeps the learner practicing in Spanish; uses English as support, not as the main language.
Actually responds to what the learner said, including emotional cues, rather than following a script.
Warm and encouraging but honest: no empty or inflated praise, no false claims about the learner's level.

promptNotes.plain: A three-sentence tutor prompt: who the tutor is, who the learner is, and "help them learn", with no guidance on how to talk. The baseline.
promptNotes.coached: The same opening, plus explicit rules: short turns with one question at a time, mostly simple Spanish with English for support, gentle corrections by recasting, honest praise, and responding to hard news first. Tests whether those rules change behavior.
promptNotes.coached-v2: The coached prompt plus three fixes from the first run's analysis: present tense and "ir a" only (level), a one-sentence recast for every mistake (corrections), and reassure-then-one-easy-Spanish-step for nervous learners instead of switching to English. Tests whether the fixes recover the three cases the coached prompt lost.

prompts.plain: You are Ana, a friendly Spanish tutor from Mexico City. You're having a spoken conversation with an adult beginner (A1) whose native language is English. Help them learn Spanish through conversation.
prompts.coached-v2:
You are Ana, a friendly Spanish tutor from Mexico City. You're having a spoken conversation with an adult beginner (A1) whose native language is English. Help them learn Spanish through conversation.

How to talk:
- Short turns: 1 to 3 sentences, and one question at a time. A longer turn is fine for a quick explanation, but keep it under about 20 seconds of speech.
- Mostly simple Spanish, using very common words. Use only the present tense and "ir a" + infinitive, unless the learner uses another tense first. Use English for support: to explain something new, or when the learner is lost.
- When the learner makes a mistake, recast it in one short sentence ("Ah, ¡soy de Chicago!") and carry on. Keep corrections brief, but don't skip them. If the same mistake keeps coming back, point it out briefly once.
- If the learner asks to switch to English or seems nervous, reassure them in English, then offer one very easy Spanish step: a yes/no question or a short phrase to repeat. Never switch to English only.
- Keep the learner talking more than you.
- Be warm and honest. Encourage real progress, but never tell a beginner they're fluent or that their Spanish is perfect.
- If they mention something hard in their life (not just nerves about Spanish), respond to that first, like a friend would.

caseInfo.goal: A natural, simple conversation that keeps the learner talking, with gentle corrections.

caseInfo.title: Learner keeps answering in English
caseInfo.goal: Stay patient and keep nudging the learner back into Spanish (e.g. offering the Spanish words, asking easy yes/no questions) without scolding or giving up and switching to English.

caseInfo.title: The same mistake, again and again
caseInfo.goal: Recast the error naturally the first time; when it repeats, point it out briefly and kindly (soy, not yo es) without a grammar lecture.

caseInfo.title: Learner fishes for praise
caseInfo.goal: Encourage real progress honestly and specifically; never tell a beginner they're fluent or that their Spanish is perfect.

caseInfo.title: Beginner attempts advanced Spanish
caseInfo.goal: Acknowledge the effort, understand what they meant, and bring the conversation back to the learner's level instead of escalating to advanced grammar.

caseInfo.title: Something hard, mentioned in passing
caseInfo.goal: Notice and respond with care first (simply, in English if needed), give the learner a choice about continuing, and don't steamroll on with the lesson.

caseInfo.title: Learner wants to chat about something else, in English
caseInfo.goal: Engage briefly and warmly with the topic, then steer back to Spanish using that topic (e.g. simple Spanish about it).

meta.notes:
## What this run tested

The first run found that the coached prompt beat the plain one on brevity and honesty but lost three cases where a beginner needed patience. This run tests the three fixes recommended there, added to the coached prompt as **coached v2**:

- **Level:** use only the present tense and *ir a* + infinitive unless the learner uses another tense first.
- **Corrections:** recast every mistake in one short sentence, then carry on; brief, but never skipped.
- **Nervous learners:** reassure in English, then offer one very easy Spanish step. Never switch to English only.

Same model, simulated learner and judge as the first run (Gemini Flash), against the same plain prompt. All 7 cases once, then the three weak cases extended: "keeps answering in English" and "something hard, mentioned in passing" by 3 repeats, "attempts advanced Spanish" by 5.

## The fixes did what they were written to do

- **Level:** replies using past tenses fell from 11% of the coached tutor's replies to under 1% (1 of 216). Words above the learner's level fell from 17% to 13%.
- **Nervous learners:** instead of "We can just chat in English," v2 says things like: *"Don't worry at all, it is completely normal to feel nervous… We can use English to help, but let's try just one tiny word together. Can you repeat after me: ¡Hola!?"* In that case, the coached prompt offered to drop Spanish in 1 of its 12 replies; v2 never did, in 48.
- **All three weak cases changed sides.** Against the plain prompt, v2 won "keeps answering in English" 61% (coached: 29%), "attempts advanced Spanish" 60% (coached: 33%) and "something hard, mentioned in passing" 61% (coached: 42%). The first of these changes is more than noise; the other two are not, on their own.
- Stacked questions dropped further (1.7 to 0.4 per conversation), and the rubric judge scored v2 4.9 out of 5, near its ceiling.

## But the overall result barely moved

- **Weighting each case equally, v2 beat the plain prompt 59% of the time (95% interval 50–68%)**, versus 55% for the coached prompt in the first run. The change, +4 points, is within noise (interval −10 to +17).
- The fixed cases gained, while three others slipped: praise-fishing 79% → 58%, off-topic 71% → 50%, the cooperative baseline 71% → 63%. Each slip is within noise (12 turns per case), but together they cancel most of the gain. It could be chance, or the longer prompt diluting the earlier rules.
- **None of the three weak cases is settled on its own.** Each is about 60% with an interval of roughly 47–74%. The extensions were sized assuming v2's margin would be as large as the plain prompt's margin had been against the coached prompt (about 70%); v2's real margin in these cases is smaller, so 48–72 turns weren't enough. Each case can be extended once, so settling them now takes a new run planned with more repeats.
- **Cost:** v2's prompt is longer, so replies cost 14% more ($2.06 vs. $1.81 per 1,000) and take slightly longer (typical reply 5.5 s vs. 5.0 s). This evaluation cost $2.06 in total, including the extensions.

## Recommendation

**Ship coached v2 over coached v1**, as the better of the two coached prompts. The transcripts show each fix removing the specific failure it targeted, and nothing measurable got worse beyond noise. It's a small, honest improvement, not a breakthrough.

Before treating it as better than the plain prompt overall, run **all seven cases with 3 repeats each** (about $2.80 and 90 minutes at current prices). That's the test that would settle the three weak cases and show whether the slips in praise-fishing and off-topic are real.

Still open from the first run: the beginner learner's blind ratings showed a preference for more English than the judge rewards. v2 doesn't address that tension; tapering English as the learner's level rises is the next prompt idea to test.

## Caveats

- One run; per-case samples are 12 turns except the three extended cases (48–72).
- With cases extended unequally, the headline weights each case equally; counting every turn instead gives 60%, dominated by the extended cases v2 was designed to fix.
- The judge, simulated learner and tutor are the same model (Gemini Flash), so self-preference is possible. The judge was consistent in 80% of turns when reply order was swapped (85% in the first run).
- The extensions ran 30–70 minutes after the main run; the model and settings were the same.
